column4: War itself finally “lays down its burdens” (تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا), joining the section’s exact وضع and وزر terms in a second image of a crushing load being put off.
The unlettered Messenger is found written in earlier scripture, and he “puts off from them their burden” (يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ); his attested mention and the removal of a load meet in one ayah.
Those who deny the meeting carry “their burdens upon their backs” (أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ), the exact bodily counter-scene to the addressee’s burden being removed from his back.
Whoever turns away from the divine reminder (ذِكْرِي) will carry a burden (وِزْرًا); rejection of dhikr produces the very load that the section sets opposite an elevated dhikr.
This ayah continues 20:100 by making people abide under that burden and calling it an evil load on Resurrection Day, so the carried وزر is enduring rather than removed.
God tells the same prophetic addressee that He will cast “a weighty word” upon him; a heavy charge placed عَلَيْكَ supplies the counter-motion to a burden later taken عَنكَ.
God “raised” the heaven and “set down” the balance (رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ ٱلْمِيزَانَ), bringing the section’s expressly opposed verbs together while keeping their objects distinct.
The revelation is “a dhikr for you and your people” (لَذِكْرٌ لَّكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ); ذِكْر and لَكَ repeat the section’s wording and present the revelation as their honor and renown.
God says He sent down a book “in which is your dhikr” (فِيهِ ذِكْرُكُمْ), making revealed speech the bearer of the community’s mention and standing.
Houses are permitted “to be raised” and God’s name “to be mentioned” in them (تُرْفَعَ وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا ٱسْمُهُ); raising and mentioning a name are coordinated acts.
The ayah begins with all honor belonging to God, then says the good word ascends and righteous action raises it; honor, utterance, and upward motion form the section’s semantic equation.
God gives Abraham and his descendants “a lofty tongue of truth” (لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا), a direct image of an honored and enduring good name granted “for them.”
Abraham asks, “Make for me a tongue of truth among later people,” stating as a prayer the lasting honorable mention that the section says God raises for someone.
“Mention in the Book Idris” makes scriptural mention the action of this ayah; 19:57 then supplies its spatially raised counterpart.
“We raised him to a high place” uses the same first-person divine action as 94:4, while 19:56 has just placed Idris in remembered speech.
After commands governing room and rising in assemblies, God raises believers and people of knowledge by degrees; the section’s dictionary image of the head of a مجلس becomes moral rank here.
The Event is “lowering, raising” (خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ), compressing the same reversal of rank into two opposed participles.
God clears Moses of what people said about him and he is distinguished in God’s sight; non-adhering blame and honored standing occur together exactly as in the section’s ظَهَرَ-based gloss.
God directly tells the Prophet that, by his Lord’s favor, he is not mad; a publicly alleged defect is kept from adhering to the addressee.
The same address then declares the Prophet to be upon tremendous character, replacing the rejected stigma of 68:2 with explicit praise.
The Prophet is promised that his Lord may raise him to “a praised station” (مَقَامًا مَّحْمُودًا), joining elevation of station to public praise.
God and the angels bless the Prophet and believers are commanded to do likewise, giving a concrete, continually repeated form to his elevated mention.
Honor belongs to God, His Messenger, and the believers; the Messenger’s standing is expressly placed on the side of عِزَّة rather than the section’s ذِلَّة.
God gives and removes dominion, honors whom He wills and humiliates whom He wills; divine elevation and ذِلَّة are presented as exact contrary changes of human standing.
In the cave scene the disbelievers’ word is made lowest while God’s word is highest, a nonlexical counterpart to lowering one thing and raising spoken mention.
Among the messengers, God speaks to some and “raises some of them by degrees,” directly applying رفع to differentiated prophetic rank.
After granting Abraham his argument, God says, “We raise by degrees whom We will,” making divinely given proof a means of elevated standing.
In Joseph’s case God says, “We raise by degrees whom We will”; the elevation follows divinely given knowledge and vindication within the narrative.
Moses prays, “My Lord, expand for me my chest” (ٱشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي), the closest repeated formulation of chest-opening with the same لِي relation.
God’s opening of a person’s chest to submission places that person upon light from his Lord, making expanded chest an inward elevation and receptivity.
God tells the Prophet that He knows his chest is constricted by what they say; hostile speech narrows the same chest whose expansion and raised mention answer it in the section.
The peoples cannot “scale” the barrier (أَن يَظْهَرُوهُ), a Qur’anic use of ظهر in the section’s developed sense “to get on top of” something.
“If they prevail over you” (إِن يَظْهَرُوا عَلَيْكُمْ) uses ظهر على in precisely the dictionary sense “overcome a person” developed in the section.
The imagined silver houses have stairways “on which they ascend” (عَلَيْهَا يَظْهَرُونَ), matching the section’s secondary ظهر sense of climbing onto a house.
God sends the Messenger with guidance and the true religion “to make it prevail over every religion”; ظهر shifts from bodily back to publicly established ascendancy.
The repeated promise that the Messenger’s true religion will be made prevailing over all religion gives public elevation to what he bears.
This third formulation of making the Messenger’s religion prevail preserves the section’s developed ظهر sense of overcoming, now applied to revealed truth.
“We left for him among later generations” gives Noah an enduring posthumous mention, the same outcome Abraham requests as a truthful tongue among later people.
“Peace upon Noah among all peoples” supplies the actual words of praise that 37:78 says were left for him.
“We left for him among later generations” realizes for Abraham the lasting mention requested in 26:84.
“Peace upon Abraham” voices the honorable remembrance whose continuance 37:108 announces.
God leaves Moses and Aaron a remembrance among later generations, extending elevated mention to another prophetic pair.
“Peace upon Moses and Aaron” gives the praise preserved by the preceding ayah rather than merely asserting fame abstractly.
God leaves Elijah a remembrance among later generations, another direct instance of a divinely preserved name.
“Peace upon Ilyasin” supplies the laudatory formula attached to the remembrance announced in 37:129.
Believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet’s voice; the physical act of رفع is bounded so that his social and prophetic standing is not violated.
The believers ask God not to lay upon them a burden as He laid on earlier people and not to load them beyond capacity, a direct prayer for the relief enacted in the section.
No bearer bears another’s burden, and if a heavily laden soul calls for help none of its load is carried; the ayah defines ownership and transfer of the load removed “from you.”
God opens the chest of one guided to submission but makes the chest of one led astray tight and constricted, as though climbing the sky; it supplies both the opening and its bodily reversal.
One who “opens his chest to disbelief” uses the same chest-opening form for the opposite moral reception, marking a boundary around expansion itself as an unqualified good.
Mockers address the recipient of “the Reminder” and call him mad; the ayah stages the attempted attachment of disgrace to the very bearer of dhikr whose mention is raised.
The Prophet’s hater is “the one cut off,” a specific reversal of lasting mention: the opponent expects the Prophet’s name to end, but the severance is assigned to the opponent.
God tells Jesus, “I am raising you to Me” and purifying him from the disbelievers; here the person is raised, clarifying by contrast the section’s careful choice to raise the name.
“Rather, God raised him to Himself” again makes a prophet, rather than his mention, the grammatical object of رفع and thus exposes the section’s object distinction.
The final home is assigned to those who do not seek elevation on earth; it distinguishes status bestowed by God from self-sought عُلُوّ.
At the Hour every pregnant one “lays down her load” (تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا); physical delivery supplies a bodily instance of وضع releasing a carried weight.
Misleaders bear their own burdens in full and some burdens of those they mislead, showing a load increased through responsibility rather than removed by grace.
The disbelievers will bear their own loads and additional loads with them, another explicit expansion of personal burden through misleading others.
“No bearer bears the burden of another” fixes the possessive boundary implicit in “your burden”: guilt belongs to its bearer unless God removes it.
The same non-transfer rule appears in a passage on guidance and accountability, sharpening why removal of one addressee’s own وزر is exceptional mercy.
“No burdened soul bears another’s burden” accompanies God’s knowledge of what is within breasts, linking accountable load and the inner person without transferring blame.
The scrolls of Moses and Abraham state that no bearer bears another’s burden, placing the load’s personal ownership within older prophetic teaching.
After purification commands, God says He does not wish to place any hardship “upon you” but to purify and complete favor; it shares the motion of withholding a constricting load from the addressee.
God has chosen the believers and placed no hardship upon them in religion; divine choosing is paired with refusing to put a constricting burden on them.
God desires to lighten for people because the human being was created weak, stating the mercy made visible when a back-breaking weight is reduced.
“Remind, for by your Lord’s favor you are neither soothsayer nor mad” couples the Prophet’s act of reminding with the removal of two public stigmas.
“Your companion is not mad” rejects an accusation against the Messenger in the audience’s own relational language, another case of blame failing to adhere.
The audience is asked whether they have reflected that there is no madness in their companion; sober recognition replaces the degrading label.
After asking the audience to reflect, the ayah says there is no madness in their companion and identifies him as a warner, clearing defect and affirming office together.
The question “Do they say there is madness in him?” is answered by his bringing them the truth, opposing attempted degradation with the worth of his message.
Those targeted by the slander are declared clear of what is said about them and promised forgiveness and noble provision, pairing non-adhering accusation with restored honor.
Those who lower their voices in the Messenger’s presence receive forgiveness and immense reward; the lowering that honors him completes the boundary set by 49:2.
God makes people successors and raises some above others in degrees “to test you,” marking bestowed rank as responsibility rather than simple prestige.
God raises some people above others in worldly degrees so they may employ one another, supplying a social and provisional sense of elevation distinct from prophetic honor.
God is “Raiser of degrees” and sends the Spirit of His command upon whom He wills, bringing elevation of rank beside the choosing of a bearer of revelation.
Joseph raises his parents upon the throne; literal placement above also publicly restores family dignity after his earlier abasement.
Moses’ next request, “make my task easy for me,” states the functional relief sought through the chest-opening of 20:25.
Moses asks that Aaron strengthen his back/support (ٱشْدُدْ بِهِ أَزْرِي), so an opened chest is joined to a back made able to bear the prophetic task.
“The foremost, the foremost” turns precedence into a named class, recalling the section’s horse that arrives ahead by its chest.
“These are the ones brought near” supplies the elevated rank that follows the precedence announced in 56:10.
Jesus announces a messenger to come after him “whose name is Ahmad,” giving the future Prophet an honorable name voiced before his own community appears.
“The earth He laid down for creatures” gives وضع a spatial object below, completing the raised heaven of 55:7 and sharpening the section’s vertical opposition.
The mother carries her child with hardship and delivers it with hardship; حمل followed by وضع makes birth an embodied instance of laying down a painfully carried load.
The waiting term lasts until pregnant women “lay down their load,” another exact use of وضع for bodily release from something carried.
God raises the mountain above the covenant people like a canopy and they think it will fall on them; the same divine “We raised” puts a massive weight overhead rather than raising a name for someone.
“We raised the Mount above you” contrasts the section’s favorable لَكَ with a heavy object raised فَوْقَكُمْ while the people are charged to hold firmly to revelation.
The repeated covenant scene again raises the Mount above the people, preserving the contrast between elevation as a threat over someone and elevation as honor for someone.
God raises the Mount above the Children of Israel for their covenant; its object and “above them” relation clarify how much the object and preposition govern the value of رفع.
God could have raised the man through His signs, but he clings to the earth and follows desire; divinely offered elevation is reversed by self-chosen abasement.

Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House while praying for acceptance; physical raising of a sacred house prepares the more explicit meeting of raised houses and remembered divine name in 24:36.
Moses says his chest constricts and his tongue does not speak freely, the felt opposite of the chest-opening he asks for in 20:25 and receives in the section’s prophetic parallel.
The Prophet’s chest is described as constricted by the opponents’ demand for treasure or an angel; their speech supplies a specific pressure answered by divine expansion and reassurance.
The sleepers warn that if their people “prevail over you” they will stone or reconvert them; ظهر على carries the developed dictionary sense of overcoming a person.
After God strengthens the believers against their enemy, they become “prevailing” (ظَاهِرِينَ), another Qur’anic realization of the section’s ظهر sense of ascendancy.
Livestock carry people’s heavy loads to a land they could reach only with severe effort, supplying a literal carrier-and-weight scene against which relief from a human back can be felt.
The Trust is offered to the heavens, earth, and mountains, which shrink from bearing it, while the human bears it; responsibility becomes a load whose acceptance can expose the bearer.
The donkey carrying books pictures revelation borne merely as weight rather than received as honor or guidance, reversing the section’s book-as-dhikr and load-removed relations.
The women confess that they know no evil of Joseph and the governor’s wife acknowledges his truthfulness, making an attached accusation fall away before his elevation.
After Joseph’s vindication, the king declares him established and trusted; cleared blame is followed by publicly raised standing in the same narrative.
God tells the same prophetic addressee that his Lord has neither forsaken nor detested him, explicitly preventing the disgrace implied by hostile or anxious speech from adhering.
“The Hereafter is better for you than the first” follows the denial of abandonment and uses لَكَ to promise an ascending valuation of the Prophet’s future.
The Lord promises to give the Prophet until he is pleased, completing 93:3–4 with positive divine favor after rejected disgrace.
Believers must not treat the Messenger’s summons among them like one another’s summons, a direct social boundary around how his call and address are honored.
Those who call the Prophet from behind the private chambers are censured as lacking understanding, a concrete misuse of address that contrasts with his elevated social standing.
God then returns the human being to the lowest of the low; here the person himself is lowered, illuminating the section’s insistence that its lowered object is the burden rather than the person.
Pharaoh exalts himself in the land and weakens one group of its people, an unethical counter-image in which self-elevation depends on pushing others down.
“The Qur’an endowed with dhikr” may carry the honor or renown sense of ذكر developed in the section, though “reminder” is also possible and makes this link uncertain.
The divine gift of abundance to the Prophet supplies the positive grant whose opposite side is the hater’s being cut off in 108:3.
Receiving one’s record from behind the back marks humiliation and impending ruin, a bodily counter-image to the section’s back relieved and name honored.
A group given scripture casts God’s book behind their backs as if they did not know; revelation that can confer dhikr is instead put at the bodily place of deliberate dishonor.
Those charged to make scripture known throw it behind their backs and trade it cheaply, reversing both public mention and honorable elevation of revealed speech.
